# ABS, Traction Control and Caution Triangle Lit Up on Dashboard

Seeing the yellow caution triangle alongside the "ABS" and "TCS" indicators permanently illuminated is a classic symptom of a specific diagnostic state in modern automotive electronics, particularly prevalent in vehicles like your 2003 Honda Accord. While you might observe that the car drives normally without these systems actively interveningâno locking brakes during hard stops, no modulation of power to wheels spinning on wet pavementâthe underlying hardware has likely reported a fault code to the Engine Control Unit (ECU).

In automotive architecture, these lights are not merely warnings; they are status outputs from the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or a dedicated Body Control Module (BCM), depending on the specific wiring harness design of that generation. When you see them lit up while the engine is running and the vehicle is in motion, it indicates that the ECU has retrieved Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) but cannot clear them automatically because the fault condition persists or the system remains in a "fail-safe" mode. The fact that functionality seems unaffected suggests the car has entered limp-home mode for those specific subsystems, allowing you to drive but disabling the safety features associated with anti-lock braking and traction stabilization.

To address this, you cannot simply reset the lights by disconnecting the battery or performing a hard reboot of the ECU, as these systems retain non-volatile memory in many architectures, or they will immediately re-illuminate upon power-up if the fault is still present. The correct approach involves reading the specific OBD-II codes stored in the system. You need an OBD-II scanner capable of reading manufacturer-specific codes, not just generic P-codes, because Honda often utilizes proprietary codes for ABS and TCS issues that standard scanners might miss or misinterpret.

Once you have the codeâfor example, a C1245 or similar code indicating a wheel speed sensor circuit issueâthe process shifts to diagnosing the physical root cause rather than attempting to "clear" the lights without fixing the trigger. The most common culprit in 2003-era vehicles is a dirty or corroded tone ring on the wheel hub, which interrupts the magnetic pickup signal sent to the ABS module. If the ECU detects an implausible wheel speed signal (e.g., one wheel spinning significantly faster than the others during deceleration), it logs the fault and illuminates the dashboard cluster.

Clearing the codes with a scanner without repairing the sensor or wiring will result in the lights returning immediately once the ignition cycle completes, because the ECU performs a self-check on startup. If the sensor signal is still invalid, the code will be set again instantly. Therefore, the technical solution is always to repair the fault: clean the tone ring, replace the wheel speed sensor, or repair any damaged wiring harnesses associated with the ABS module.

There is a nuance regarding the "caution triangle" light appearing alongside these indicators. In many Honda models from this era, this specific combination often points to a failure in the communication between the ABS module and the main ECU, or a general system fault that encompasses both braking stability and traction control logic. If the communication bus (CAN bus) is functioning but the sensor data is corrupted, the system disables active intervention to prevent unsafe behavior, leaving the lights on as a persistent reminder of the disabled safety layer.

If you choose to proceed with code clearing before repair, be aware that this is generally considered a temporary workaround rather than a solution. It may pass an immediate visual inspection, but the lack of ABS and TCS means your stopping distances will increase significantly in emergency scenarios, and wheel lock-up remains a risk on low-traction surfaces. The only definitive way to extinguish these lights permanently is to resolve the hardware fault that generated the DTCs in the first place. If the issue persists after sensor replacement and code clearing, you may need to inspect the ABS pump and motor assembly for internal faults or check the fuse and power supply to the ABS module itself.
